choices.C: A public key to the verified identity of its owner, signed by a trusted CA

questions.explanation: An X.509 certificate contains the subject's public key, identity, and the CA's digital signature confirming identity verification.

questions.stem: Which PKI entity signs certificates to vouch for the holder's identity?
questions.explanation: A CA is the trusted third party that verifies identity claims and signs certificates. Trust in the certificate derives from trust in the CA.

questions.stem: Certificate revocation marks a certificate as:

choices.D: No longer trusted before its expiry date, due to key compromise or CA error

questions.explanation: Revocation invalidates a certificate before its scheduled expiry, typically due to private key compromise. Status is published via CRL or OCSP.

choices.A: Providing a pre-computed list of all revoked certificates
choices.C: Enabling real-time per-certificate status checks without downloading a full CRL
choices.D: Eliminating the need for a CA

questions.explanation: OCSP allows clients to query a specific certificate's status in real time, more efficient and current than downloading and parsing a full CRL.

questions.explanation: A wildcard covers first-level subdomains (mail.example.com, api.example.com) but not the apex (example.com) or multi-level subdomains.

questions.explanation: HSTS instructs browsers to always use HTTPS for a domain, refusing HTTP connections and preventing SSL stripping attacks.

questions.stem: Certificate pinning in a mobile app means:

choices.B: The certificate is cached locally on the device
choices.D: The app only accepts a specific certificate or public key hash, rejecting others even if CA-signed

questions.explanation: Certificate pinning hardcodes the expected certificate or key hash. Even a valid CA-signed certificate is rejected if it doesn't match the pin.

questions.stem: An internal CA's certificates are trusted only by:

choices.A: All internet users via the public root CA store
choices.B: All systems globally via X.509 universal trust
choices.D: Devices configured to explicitly trust the internal root CA certificate

questions.explanation: Internal CA certificates use a root not in public trust stores. Only devices to which the root has been deployed and installed will trust them.

choices.A: That the applicant controls the domain name, no organisational identity verification
choices.B: Full legal identity and physical address of the organisation
choices.C: Extended legal entity information over several days
choices.D: That the site uses minimum TLS 1.2

questions.explanation: DV certificates verify domain control only (via DNS record or file placement). No legal entity verification is performed, fastest to obtain, lowest assurance.

questions.stem: Mutual TLS (mTLS) differs from standard TLS in that:

choices.A: Both server AND client present and verify certificates, providing two-way authentication
choices.C: mTLS encrypts only the server's response
choices.D: mTLS does not require a CA

questions.explanation: Standard TLS authenticates only the server. mTLS requires both parties to present valid certificates, used for API-to-API and service mesh authentication.
